rows.grounds: locative adverb referring to the wave state

items.question: Is the essential nature of water destroyed when waves arise?
premises: Waves are transient forms of water.
The underlying water-nature persists through wave formation.
Destruction of a form does not entail destruction of its essence.
items.inference: The water-nature is not destroyed at the time of waves.
items.plain_english: And there, at the time of the waves, there is no destruction of the water's essential form.

rows.grounds: refers to the water or its state

items.question: Does differentiation by waves imply a special distinction belonging to motionlessness?
premises: An objection may claim waves distinguish water from stillness.
A distinction attributed to waves would mark motionlessness as a special state.
The analogy tests whether form alters essential nature.
items.inference: If water were distinguished by waves, that distinction would belong to motionlessness.
items.plain_english: If that is distinguished by the waves, then that would be a special mark of motionlessness.

rows.grounds: concludes the hypothetical from previous verse
applies the analogy to the main case
in the state of manifest existence

items.question: Does Śiva-nature remain established even when reality assumes manifest forms?
premises: The water-wave analogy shows essence persists through changing forms.
Manifest existence corresponds to the arising of forms.
Śiva-nature is the underlying essence of all manifestation.
items.inference: Even in the state of manifest form, Śiva-nature remains established.
items.plain_english: Thus, even in the state of manifest existence, Śiva-ness remains firmly established.

rows.grounds: the quality of being inert or unconscious

items.question: What follows if insentience is perceived in the group of principles beginning with earth?
premises: The tattvas from earth onward are commonly taken as insentient.
This perception raises an objection against universal Śiva-nature.
The objection must be addressed within the nondual framework.
items.inference: The apparent insentience of lower tattvas poses a challenge to be resolved.
items.plain_english: If insentience is perceived in the group of principles beginning with earth,

items.question: Can the ultimate reality be considered composite anywhere despite apparent insentience in tattvas?
premises: The author promises to explain the objection regarding insentience.
A composite nature would imply division and limitation.
Ultimate reality cannot be divided into parts.
items.inference: The reality in question is not composite anywhere.
items.plain_english: We shall indeed explain this here: and it is not composite anywhere.

rows.grounds: by its own freedom; sandhi: svecchātaḥ

items.question: How could a state arising from its own will be dependent on another?
premises: Manifestation occurs by the reality's own will.
Dependence on another implies limitation of freedom.
What arises freely cannot be externally constrained in its essence.
items.inference: A state assumed by its own will cannot be dependent on another.
items.plain_english: When it assumes manifest form by its own will, how could its state be dependent on another?

rows.grounds: by the same line of reasoning; sandhi: etayā+eva
to be cleared away or corrected

items.question: By what method should objections concerning purity and deficiency be refuted?
premises: The preceding reasoning establishes freedom and non-compositeness.
Objections about purity or deficiency arise from misunderstanding manifestation.
The same principle applies to all such alleged faults.
items.inference: By this very line of reasoning, objections of purity, deficiency, and the like are to be refuted.
uncertainties: The exact scope of 'śuddhanyūnādi' depends on the specific objections in context.
items.plain_english: By this very line of reasoning, the fault alleged in terms of purity, deficiency, and so on, is to be refuted.

rows.grounds: in states like falling, being grasped, etc.
in forms like a crown, etc.

items.question: Does gold lose its essential nature when shaped into a crown or subjected to other conditions?
premises: Gold undergoes various modifications and uses.
A crown is a particular form taken by gold.
The essential nature of a substance persists through its modifications.
items.inference: Gold-ness remains in gold whether in a crown or in other conditions.
items.plain_english: In gold, whether falling, being seized, or fashioned into a crown and so on, its gold-ness remains.

rows.grounds: fire present in an outcaste's dwelling; sandhi: caṇḍāla+sadma+gaḥ

items.question: Why might fire in an outcaste's house be conventionally denied the name of fire?
premises: Fire retains its essential nature regardless of location.
Scriptural or social conventions may restrict naming based on context.
Such restrictions concern usage, not the essence of the thing.
items.inference: Fire in an outcaste's house may be said not to be fire by convention, though its nature is unchanged.
items.plain_english: Fire that has gone to an outcaste's house is said, 'it is not fire.'

rows.grounds: for the sake of a practical effect; sandhi: kārya+artham
refers to the designation or rule

items.question: For what purpose do scriptures describe such conventional distinctions?
premises: Scriptures sometimes make distinctions that do not reflect essential nature.
Practical effects and ritual outcomes guide conventional usage.
The distinction serves a functional purpose rather than an ontological one.
items.inference: Such scriptural descriptions are made for the sake of practical effect alone.
items.plain_english: Why is this described in the scriptures? It is indeed for the sake of a practical effect.

items.question: What is the status of distinctions that are merely matters of naming?
premises: Some distinctions are created only for practical communication.
Naming does not alter the underlying essence of things.
Conventional use requires stipulated designations.
items.inference: That is merely a matter of naming, contrived for conventional use.
items.plain_english: That is merely a matter of naming, contrived for conventional use.

rows.grounds: refers to the distinction or designation

items.question: What role do mere names play in the conduct of worldly life?
premises: Worldly conduct depends on shared conventions.
Names and distinctions facilitate practical interaction.
Such conventions do not determine ultimate reality.
items.inference: For worldly conduct, that becomes merely a contrived name.
items.plain_english: For the conduct of worldly life, that becomes merely a contrived name.
